utterances.text: Mr. Eric, in the English translation the list speaks of public security station, and the signature of Bogdanovic Luka speaks of militia station commander. Now, what does it mean, the -- to my mind that is somehow a difference between the name of the list, public security station, and the signature of Bogdanovic. Has it been the same unit or has there been different organisations which corroborated in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the same unit. This is the public security station. He must have been the police commander, the commander of the police itself, the building itself was referred to as the public security station. I guess that's how it was. I'm not sure I can really explain this fully. I've never been a member of the police. Therefore, I'm not exactly clear about these things myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the late Milutin Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that he was the chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that on the 29th of May, 1992, there was fierce fighting going on, and Milutin Milosevic was killed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on to my next question, I move that this previous document be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It will certainly be assigned a number. May I ask you a question, Madam Vidovic. The document itself, starting on 01320218, basically indicates or gives us a list of employees who performed duties at the public security station during the month of April and who should be paid in advance for this month.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you explain that? Because it seems that what we have here is payment in advance for the month of May. Is that correct or not? In other words, I take it that whatever was due to them for the month of April had already been settled and what is being shown on the document is what they should be paid in advance for the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document is from the financial records of the Bratunac Brigade, personal income in relation to May 1995. And the number is 01320145. It is true, though, that the document itself, the document itself, is a list of employees that carried out their duties throughout the month of April, and these are to be paid in advance. This is what they choose to call it. Where I come from, when you speak about an advance, you can mean different things. Sometimes advances were paid in relation to different periods of time. For about half a year, and then later the rest would be paid. So that's that. Maybe they had certain sums of money at their disposal at the time and then later the differences between these amounts were also paid. But as I said, this is a document from the financial records of the Bratunac Brigade for May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, I have an additional question. Would you please put on the ELMO, Madam Usher, the page 3 of the original. If you look to numbers 95 to numbers 106, or even 107, you get the impression that you have the same signature, signature of the same person. Now, how can it be explained that you have the same signature? So was it a lump sum for a couple of people who --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's possible that one person picked up salaries for people close to them, for friends, and signed for them that they had taken these amounts of money, and then later distributed it to the people in question. This is not something that is unusual. It happens where we come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Registrar, this document is being tendered by --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Before you continue, I just want to put a couple of Prosecution objections on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would just like to note that the first page of this exhibit appears to be a handwritten page translated into the date of May 1992, and that if you would look at the rest of the document that's in Bosnian language, it appears to be typewritten completely, and I see no indication that 1992, that year, in any of the parts that are typewritten, only a reference to what has been translated as April, and neither is there a date after the signature on the -- under the seal of the typewritten part. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the first point raised by Ms. Sellers. We have two parts to this document that you seek to tender, Madam Vidovic, and on the face of it, at least, they don't seem to be -- or to belong to the same document. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first part of the document is this cover page, the first page, of the entire financial documentation from May 1992, precisely as it was disclosed to us by the Prosecution. It's a document of over 100 pages. So it's the same way that it was disclosed by the Prosecution. And I brought this cover page. Not only for this month; two or three days ago, we had documents for November 1992 disclosed, and similarly, there's a handwritten page for November, while the rest of the document are typewritten pages. So we are presenting it in the same way that it was disclosed to us. And I am using it in the same way. If the Prosecutor doubts or suspects that the Defence did some additional work on these documents, I can then present the entire document for personal salaries for May 1992, just as it was disclosed to us. They disclosed that same document on EDS, in the same form that I'm using it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second point raised is -- or would require you to explain on what basis you come to the conclusion that the rest of the document, starting on 01320218 and finishing ending on three pages later, after, 1320221, refers to April 1992 and not to April of any other year. Because there doesn't seem to be anything on these four pages that could be indicative of the year to which the document refers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document, because of the death of Milutin Milosevic, who was killed in May 1992, must refer to this month. But I repeat: That part of the financial documentation of the Bratunac Brigade was disclosed to us as part of a hundred-page document for May 1992, and this, these pages, are part of that document. But if you allow me, perhaps I can ask the witness some questions in reference to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So one moment before you proceed, Madam Vidovic, because we have to get this sorted out. The position as we see it is as follows: It seems, and there is no reason for us to doubt that, that this document forms part of a larger document which was disclosed by the Prosecutor herself to the Defence. So according to what has been explained to us by Madam Vidovic, this single page should form part of that document, and the other four pages, although they are not sequentially following the previous page, should form part of the same document. We have also taken note of the point raised by you that there is nothing on the face of this document barring page 1 that is indicative or could be indicative that we're talking of April 1992, and not some other year. That is true as well. But we have also taken note of what has been submitted by Madam Vidovic, namely, that Milosevic Milutin was killed in May of that year. So it couldn't possibly refer to post-April 1992. Admittedly, it could refer to pre-1992. I suppose that once you have the entire document at your disposal, because it's you who have handed it over to the Defence, you can check that. If you have further reasons to doubt any of the matters or the points that we have tried to clear, then you will let us know. In the meantime, we are admitting this document and we are marking it as D1 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D127.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, it is correct that on the 29th of May, 1992 the late Mr. Milutin Milosevic was killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I -- I haven't -- I haven't heard Mr. Eric answer the question. And in fact, in the transcript, there is nothing. Mr. Eric, is it true --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not saying -- speaking loudly because of you. I didn't want to disturb you, so that's why I said it quietly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Disturb who? Could you answer the question now, please. Is it correct that on the 29th of May, 1992, Mr. Milutin Milosevic was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a large and coordinated action of the TO forces of Kravica, and the police forces under the command of Milosevic, which on that day attacked the Muslim village of Sandici, with the intention of cleansing it; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. They were going to pull out the personnel carrier that was left behind. It wasn't about Sandici. There was a transporter going towards Milici that encountered a barricade, an ambush, and I don't know whether it was going towards Pervane or something. I think that's what it's about, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose transporter was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: It was a Serbian vehicle, an armoured combat vehicle. I'm not sure what the exact name of it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the Kravica forces had an armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, you are not allowing an interval after Madam Vidovic's questions. Please allow a short interval of time, because the interpreters will find it difficult to catch up with you. Yes. My apologies to you, Madam Vidovic. Please move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose APC was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: It belonged to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask that the witness be shown Defence Exhibit D123.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at this list. It is the list of those killed in Sandici. Do you agree, could you please look at the list. The first 11 people were killed on the 29th of May, 1992, in Sandici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the name under number 3, Milutin Milosevic, son of Stevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is Mr. Milosevic Milutin, the chief of the public security station. It's true, isn't it, that he was killed in Sandici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think he was caught alive and I think that they killed him. Yes, he was killed. He was caught alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, could you please reply only to my questions. Is it true that he was killed on the 29th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already told us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer of the witness because he was speaking at the same time as the translation was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has told us already about three or four times that Milutin Milosevic was killed on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, you're a medical technician and a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that many people from Serbia and the Serbian Krajina in Croatia were killed in the Kravica front?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, not many. There were some, but not many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look once again at this list.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: This list? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at the names of these people and see where they come from.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 29th, several people were killed who are not from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Eric. I would like to ask you something else now. Your close cousin, relative, is Golub Eric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is my grandfather's brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that his real name is Bogoljub?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Isn't it true that before the attack on the 7th of January, before the January events, the events of January 1993, the majority of women, children, and elderly men, or the infirm, were moved out from the Kravica area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And mostly fighters remained in that area; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Ranging from 15 to 80 years of age, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony last time, you said that the Kravica area did not have large quantities of weapons. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, not major quantities, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, actually, that Kravica was a Serbian stronghold, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you permit me, I would just like to clarify this with a couple of words.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask him questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, could you please kindly answer the question whether it was a stronghold, Serbian stronghold or not, with a yes or a no. Then if you need to explain something else, you need to tell us what you need to explain and why you need to explain it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely in support of this question, I actually wanted to clarify certain things. I'm here in this Tribunal for the second time now, and I have noticed that the Prosecution wants to prove that Kravica was actually an unprotected, undefended Serbian village. And the Defence, on the other hand, wants to say that it was a strong Serbian stronghold. Gentlemen, Kravica was not one thing or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How strong and fortified it was, how fortified was it when it was taken in one day? It's not Vukovar, which took months to be conquered. So you can see how strong it was and how many weapons it had, based on this. But I apologise. This is something that I just wanted to say in relation to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic, does that satisfy your question or would you like to put the same question again? Because was it a Serbian stronghold could have more than one meaning. So if you want to proceed with the question, rephrasing it, possibly, you have our permission to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to show the witness a number of documents, and we will discuss it in that way. I would now like to ask the usher to show the witness Defence Exhibit D5. Your Honour, this is a document that is also a part of the financial documentation of the Bratunac Brigade, and it's an extract from the record of personnel salaries for May 1992 and it's a list of the people in the Territorial Defence of Donji Magasici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at page 01320152.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Donji Magasici is a village from the Kravica local commune?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the section here referring to the type of weapon, and you can see the markings there, PM. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a marking for a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that AP --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Is the marking for an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that M-48 is also a mark indicating a rifle?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this, I would like to ask you the following: A small place, such as Magasici Donji, had 56 pieces of different weapons, including automatic weapons and machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other villages in the Kravica area received the same amounts of weapons, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, there were such villages, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The local units received substantial support from the volunteers who came from Serbia and the Croatian Krajina at the beginning of the war who originally hailed from the Kravica area. Was this not the case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases like that, people who worked in Serbia, and when the war broke out, they came to the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now please be shown the following document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Vidovic, if this cross-examination is bound to continue for a long time, may we please have a break, because I would like to go and use the facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure if you've taken notice. The witness needs a break, and he wants to know how much longer I'll go on for. I think about 25 minutes, but it appears that he needs a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll certainly give the witness a short break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you please escort the witness, and we'll wait here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, so as not to waste time, Mr. Jones, you informed the Trial Chamber earlier on in the day that you had some submissions to make in relation to the next witness. How long do you anticipate would that take you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I didn't plan to actually make the submissions orally. We filed a motion today, I mean in the last break, and it concerns an exhibit which we understand the Prosecution may intend to use with the next witness. And it's our application that that should be excluded. What's probably best is if I distribute courtesy copies of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, because we are not even aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, indeed, I only filed it moments ago, and I have courtesy copies available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And which document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a video which is designated as V0002554, and transcripts of the video. The video has not yet been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But it has been pre-marked as P97 and P98.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Siller, please follow me. According to the information that I have, because I do have it here, this video has been pre-marked as P97 and P98. It's V0002554. Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have something else for P97. That could be an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Because Judge Eser is pointing out that this video with 0002554 is P448, which was run before, which was run before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we must be -- or rather, you must be talking of some other video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's certainly not a video which has been run already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Then it cannot be V0002554. Usher, any time the witness is ready, bring him over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But also in the list, in the Prosecution list of description of exhibits that are going to be used, P448 is described as V0002554, which is definitely not the same video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: P448 is I think V0002774. I think there must be an error somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could help you. That was the video that we saw earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's P448. That's P448, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. And this is the one ending 2554 and as far as we understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, if you could provide us with a courtesy copy of your motion, please, so that will be prepared for the discussion as soon as we finish with this witness. Yes. Are you feeling okay, Mr. Eric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have any problems at any time and would like a break, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I don't think I will need any further breaks. Just this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just please look at this document, military post 7042 Bratunac, and the mark is 013210091, and the date is the 29th of September, 1993. This is a record, a list of soldiers who were killed, of a soldier who was killed. Can you please have a look. The name is Miroslav Marincevic, volunteer, born 1965 in Nis. It is true, isn't it, that Nis is a town in Serbia; therefore, this person does not hail from the Kravica area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: This is not a person I knew. I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look further down the page. We have the date and place of death, the 17th of December, 1992, seriously wounded in Siljkovici on the 18th of December, he died in hospital in Belgrade. And the manner of death, in combat, and then there is a remark further down the page: "While carrying out combat operations, the above-named was seriously wounded."

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: It was probably in some shooting or as part of an attack, I assume, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore you agree with me, don't you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I just want to say that at this point these are the types of documents that we saw when Mr. Eric was called the first time. I'm waiting to see how the Defence is tying this specifically back to the video, and I would just like to remind the Trial Chamber we thought the basis of the further cross-examination were things that specifically appeared on the video and weren't known. And I would like to state that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think what you're stating for the record is very relevant. Madam Vidovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may reply. We did not see these documents. As for the video, Mr. Rasa Milanovic, the whole video, and the last time we did not get a transcript from the OTP, let me put that on the record, but in the video, he speaks about precisely what I'm asking the witness about now, the arrival of volunteers from Serbia and the Croatian Krajina. And he says that he personally arrived from the front in Croatia. Therefore, this is highly relevant. Your Honour, I have the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Madam Vidovic. The Trial Chamber doesn't really agree with you that this is highly relevant. It only says where he was born. It doesn't say where he was residing before he was killed in Siljkovici. Let's proceed, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I move that this document be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document is being tendered, admitted and marked as Defence Exhibit 128.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, in addition to the local units in the Kravica area, from the very outset of the war in 1992, various units were also stationed, units that were made up of people who were not locals or resided in the area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance again, please, to show another document to the witness. This is a Bratunac military post, 0132127. This is also a record sheet of a soldier who was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Witness, can you have a look.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: There is nothing for me to look at here. It's pointless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take it easy, please. The name is Ratko Visnjic, volunteer, killed on the 7th of January, 1993, in Siljkovici, member of a special unit of the MUP. My question --

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Please, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please can the witness answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's fine, Your Honour. I'll answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you tried this already on the 26th of October, and if you try to do it again now, today, here, you will incur disciplinary measures on the part of the Trial Chamber. Madam Vidovic is doing her duty here, and you are a witness, and you are a witness, and you have to respect the Rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... will ask the questions, to put the questions to you, and just restrict yourself to answering the questions. And no comments and no gestures. Because you will regret everything that you do otherwise. Madam Vidovic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior, the abbreviation is MUP, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, a police unit, a special MUP unit, this is a special MUP unit of Republika Srpska, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: If you remember my last testimony --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Please allow me to explain. This special unit of the MUP from Bijeljina was in Kravica. It came and stayed for about 10 or 15 days before Kravica burned down. This man was born in Sarajevo. What sort of a volunteer is he supposed to be, where from? He can't possibly be considered a volunteer. He resided in Sarajevo which is the former Republic of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. Is it true, then, that this special unit of the MUP of Republika Srpska was stationed in the Kravica area during the events in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: There was a minor unit. I'm not sure what the name was, from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers. One moment, because I'm sure that the interpreters didn't catch what you were going to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe from looking back on the transcript that the witness ever agreed that the MUP was from the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. He's never agreed that -- in fact, he said that this was a special unit in Kravica or -- he explained, but he never mentioned that it was -- or agreed that it was part of the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have no idea what the name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a special unit of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I really don't know. They had uniforms that looked more like military uniforms to me. I really don't know who exactly they were. I don't think I can answer that question. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just -- well, before I ask anything, can this document please be assigned a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. This document is being assigned Defence Exhibit number D129.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see a document here. It's a Bratunac Brigade document. The number is 01322160, dated the 2nd of January, 1993. I will quote briefly. It says: "24 plus 2 plus 4 men were brought in from Serbia (with or without weapons). 23 men handed over to Captain Vaso Gujic in Glogova to be deployed at the positions. Soldiers who did not have any weapons signed for weapons that were confiscated in Serbia. On the same day, 17 light-barrelled weapons were seized in Serbia. In the military police depot, there are still three light machine-guns and ten light-barrelled weapons, snipers." In relation to that, let me ask you the following question: Is it true that the position in Glogova in December 1992 and January 1993, a position under the command of Captain Vaso Gujic was deployed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last time around, Mr. Eric, when we spoke on the 26th of October, 2004, on page 1247, last line, and then running on to the following page, lines 1, 2, and 3, I quote: "It is a duty of the medical worker to be familiar with the positions of the units and personnel holding those positions." Therefore, you were aware of the positions held by those units. It is true, isn't it, that Captain Vaso Gujic was a professional officer, a Serb, originally from Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I simply don't know this person. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question. Did Glogova come under your area of responsibility or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from Kravica towards Bratunac, but not from the other side, from Bratunac. As far as I understand, we are speaking about the direction of Bratunac. This man, Vaso Gujic, as you said, if he was in Bratunac, then he was not in Kravica, not on our side, because then I would know who he was. I would have seen him there with the army. It was my duty to know who was around.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try to rephrase the question. Mr. Eric, is it not true that the positions in Jezestica are linked to the positions in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Magasici and Jezestica are nearby, so they're adjacent. Jezestica and Magasici. Magasici is adjacent to Glogova, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm saying, Mr. Eric, that this unit was precisely at those positions which continue on from Magasici towards Glogova. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. On the side of Bratunac. That's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the Kravica area, refugees from Zenica and Srebrenica fought in that area under the command of a professional officer, a Serb man who comes from Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: They were not refugees. They had arrived in 1992. They were together with us. They lived in Bratunac. Some of them are in Bratunac to this very day. They fought at our lines, and many of them were killed. That's true. They were all over, but there were some also in Bratunac. Yes, they were expelled from Central Bosnia, then they were refugees. They'd been with us from 1992. It's been ten years now. Those who remained are now people from Bratunac. They are no longer refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Eric. I will just briefly ask you the following: Is it true that in the Kravica area, in late December and early January 1993, there was also the special guards which fought in that area; they were called Panthers, from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. They used to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Did it fight in that area in early January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move to my next question, I would just like to have this previous document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will be D1 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will be document D130. I notice that the transcript shows D1. It should be D130.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, we are now going to show you another document. This is an excerpt from a report and from notes of the Bratunac Brigade, 0132207. The date is the 7th of January, 1993. Mr. Eric, can you please look at this document. I will now quote from it: "On the 7th of January, 1993, in the early morning hours, an attack was launched on Kravica from all sides. Immediately upon being informed, the commander engaged the available forces and sent them to Kravica to assist. The military police dispatched 14 people, with weapons and equipment who had been in detention for abandoning positions and other disciplinary offences. The list of military conscripts is located in the records with the duty-officer in the military police. At around 730 hours I requested information about the members of the military police who are deployed in the Kravica area." And then my question is in relation to this, Mr. Eric. You were in Kravica at the time of the attack, weren't you? Therefore, it is true that a number of different units fought there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Different? In what way? They all took part in the defence of the village, all the units that were there. Therefore, I'm not sure what you mean by saying "different."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these units that we spoke about today also fight, including the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know. After 10.00, I received no information whatsoever. I have no idea if they were there or not. It's possible, but as far as I can see, based on this document, they were not there. Up to 1000 hours, I had not received any information in the Kravica/Njive sector. Therefore -- because the Muslim units in the area were making the fastest progress. That would be an answer for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document is being tendered and received as a Defence exhibit, and is being marked as Defence Exhibit D131.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I have no objections to the document. Just we'd note that it doesn't seem to have a signature, it doesn't seem to have any official indication of where it comes from, although learned counsel, learned friend, has testified where she thinks that this has come from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Point taken. Madam Vidovic, do you have any further information?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to reply? My learned friend and colleague did not give her opinion on where she thinks the document comes from. She appears quite certain. However, this document is from a set of documents in relation to the Bratunac Brigade disclosed to us by the OTP. It's part of the set that was disclosed as the notes of the Bratunac Brigade, and this is merely an excerpt from the following document. Therefore, Your Honours, should there be any further objections like this to these documents, I will see myself compelled to bring along documents that sometimes run into hundreds of pages. The source for these documents is the OTP, including everything concerning where the documents came from and how they came into the possession of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Excuse me. I do take note of what Madam Vidovic is saying, learned counsel, I'm just merely noting that this specific document, not the collection it's come from, but that there's no indication on the handwritten document as to who wrote it or any official seal. I'm quite aware that the Bratunac collection has provided Defence with many of the documents that they're using. That is certainly not our objection. Our objection has to deal more specifically with the contents, but also the specific document in its identification as to who wrote it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it clear, because the first thing that Ms. Sellers had said when she rose to raise an objection was precisely that she was not objecting to the document itself. And you're taking it that she was objecting to the document itself. I think we will need to take objections as and if and when they arise and take it up from there. On the other hand, I also wish to make it clear that the fact that a document has been in the possession of the Prosecution and then in addition has been forwarded to the Defence, does not prevent the Prosecution from contesting the admissibility of the document. So at the end of the day, there is no reason why we should create an incident out of this. And let's move forward. Next question, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, does this mean that this document will not be assigned a number? I'm not sure I understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have already -- I have already assigned a number to it. I said it is D131.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, I will just ask you a couple of questions. Today you were asked about the contacts between Kravica and the Milici Brigade. Is it true that in Milici that the Milici Brigade, the Milici Light Brigade was in fact based in Milici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it must have been. I never went to that brigade, but I can't think where else it could have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also true, Mr. Eric, that the main depot, warehouse, for the ammunition and weapons used for the entire Birca area was located there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that on the 7th of January, 1993, 49 fighters were killed in the Kravica area who were from Kravica and 38 of them were wounded?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have accurate information on this. I do, however, believe that what you say is correct. It certainly sounds accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true, Mr. Eric, isn't it, that in the videotape you said that 38 people had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I can't be positive about that. Maybe 37 or perhaps more. But the number is -- the figure is certainly a relevant one, generally speaking. Am I making myself clear?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'll just ask you one more question. On the tape, you mentioned that you had expected a helicopter to arrive.

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who promised that to you? Who promised to send over the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: If you remember my previous testimony, I said that once or twice in the course of that day, I nipped over to the command that was at the school building and one of the people who were there told me. Who specifically it was, I really have no idea. It was a long time ago. I really can't say who specifically. Someone over there said to me something like: Just take it easy. A helicopter has been promised to be sent over and evacuate the wounded. And Mile would be sending APCs. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, someone who was a member of the command staff at the school building in Kravica promised you this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get your logistics from for your own duties, Mr. Eric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: For my duties, you mean the medical staff? At the beginning of the war, we had our own reserves at the hospital. And then if you remember from the transcript the last time around, a van full of medicine was sent over from Holland and then we were using that for a while, and later we relied on the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you about the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993? Where were you getting your logistics from, as a medical worker?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Mostly from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be allowed. May I just say a couple of words in relation to my previous testimony? I would just like to show you a couple of statements that I made to newspapers, statements that were used by the Defence, statements I made to a variety of daily papers in Bosnia and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, the witness said that the Defence had used something. This Defence never in any way talked to anyone outside this courtroom about this specific witness or this trial. Therefore, I think it is impermissible for the witness to be making a statement like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have proof. Madam Vidovic, is this you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Eric --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- here in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You do not address Madam Vidovic directly. I prohibit you from addressing Madam Vidovic directly, unless you are authorised by the Trial Chamber. So what articles or documents do you want to show the Trial Chamber? Let's see what they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you remember the last time I testified, the Defence asked me: Mr. Eric, is it not true that your two grandfathers, Negoslav [phoen] and Golub, for the crimes they committed against the Muslim people, were convicted to long terms of imprisonment? If you remember, my reply to the Defence at the time was as follows: They were not sentenced to long terms of imprisonment, but rather, they were sentenced to be shot, and they had served their long-term prison sentences already. And then there is an article in a newspaper called Dnevni Avaz. I find this article which reads: "Witness Slavisa Eric confirms the crimes of his grandfather, Golub." What exactly is this supposed to mean? I should like to ask the Defence. What was the meaning behind this newspaper article, and what was I supposed to answer in reply to their question? If I had sworn here to tell the truth, and the truth is that my grandfathers were sentenced to a death by firing squad. And the link between myself and my grandfathers is the same that the link is going to be one day between my children and my present testimony. I don't think this was a fair move. Both myself and my family were damaged by this. It would not surprise me at all if suddenly one day I turned up on the front page of this newspaper called Dnevni Avaz. It would not surprise me in the least, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. The witness's testimony was given in public session. If a newspaper decides to report, either accurately or inaccurately, on the testimony which was given, that's got absolutely nothing to do with the Defence. The question was properly put, it was put in the context of there being very old fighters in Kravica, which, as you know has been an issue in this trial as to whether certain people are combatants or not, and it's obviously entirely improper for a witness to come here and to wave newspaper articles around and seek to accuse the Defence on that basis. So I strongly object to the witness being heard any! More.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does anyone know who Mr. A. Hadzic is? Do you know who Mr. Hadzic is? Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a lady journalist of the Avaz newspaper. However, Your Honour, I must say that I never made any public statements disclosing any details of this trial to anyone at any time, and I don't think, frankly, that that is what this newspaper article reflects, in addition to which, I know that quite many journalists from Bosnia-Herzegovina are following this trial, and some may even be sitting behind the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is this newspaper published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Naturally, there is very little we can say at this point in time, because this is in your own language, which we don't understand. We'll give instructions to have it translated, at least for our information, and we'll come back to the Trial Chamber -- or the Trial Chamber will come back on this if it is at all necessary. Otherwise, we will just put it on record and that will be the end of it. Mr. Eric -- Madam Sellers, are there any further questions on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We'll have no re-examination at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Judge Eser -- Judge Brydensholt. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, I understood that on the day of the 7th of January you were in contact with commandants of the units which were placed in the school, in the headquarter there. You had some connection with them. Were you aware if there in the same school building was a deposit of arms? You were very close to them. What kind of a deposit, if any, was there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: There was ammunition stored there, but it was not really a depot. It wasn't far from the medical centre. The distance was perhaps 200 or 300 metres. So I would just walk over or run across between the houses to see what was going on, because I didn't know. I worked inside a room. So that's when they told me. But it was not really an ammunition depot in the proper sense of the word, containing explosives and mines. If that had been the case, when there was an explosion, when the school building caught fire, the whole thing would have gone up in smoke. It wouldn't have just remained standing. It would have exploded, the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: One more question. Were you aware that a tank was placed in the school yard?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. No. No, there was no tank. I don't think we even had a tank. It was an APC, an old one. I don't think it was a tank. An APC or something along these lines, and it stayed right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This APC, did it have a gun mounted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: A Browing 12.7 millimetres. It's a heavy machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Eric, you have been asked for the military unit, and you have been asked what it was. Am I remembering correctly that you told us you didn't know what it was, what the militia brigade meant? You have been asked for the nature of this Brigade in Milici, and to my recollection, you answered you did not know the nature of this unit or brigade or whatever you may call it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: The brigade. Well, the brigade was in Bratunac. My apologies. We were more some sort of a battalion at that time, around Christmas-time, between 300 and 400 people. It's a battalion, establishment-wise. Bratunac had a brigade which was made up of Kravica, then the area closer to Srebrenica. And then on the other side, two, three, or four battalions. I think that's how many it had. This was a battalion-strong unit, in fact. At the outset, it was some sort of Territorial Defence detachment. I'm not even sure what to call it or what it was. I don't think anyone knows. And then as people were being killed and as people were leaving, the unit grew smaller and became some sort of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And a little earlier you had been asked by -- I think by the Defence with regard to reinforcements coming from Milici. And you answered that this reinforcement did not come, but it was expected. Now, what did you expect from them? What type of help did you expect from them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVISA ERIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, to break through to where we were and to help us defend ourselves, to link up with us across Kostan to reach Kravica. But they were ambushed at Siljkovici and they were prevented from reaching us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. Mr. Eric, that brings your testimony to an end. You will be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher. Once more, I should like to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser and myself, also on behalf of the Tribunal, for having accepted to return to this Tribunal to continue or to resume and finish your evidence after the discovery of the video that was mentioned earlier. I would also like to wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Thank you. And please bear me no grudges. I have never faced any kind of Tribunal before. I have no record whatsoever, not even for a traffic offence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, the courtesy copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I have them here. While I remember, Your Honour, might we have a copy at some stage of that newspaper article as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Registrar, please, make a photo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Copies for the Prosecution, for the Defence, and for us, but we need the translation more than -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Please be prepared to discuss the merit of this urgent motion, first and foremost, before we admit the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And you'll see there's a correction in the first paragraph, line 6. I've done that by hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I saw Ms. Richardson. For the record, Ms. Richardson has joined the Prosecution team. Yes. There is this urgent motion that the Defence has filed. I would imagine that you may have something to say about it, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. First, just to say that we've clarified, I think, the question of exhibit numbers. Our understanding was that the transcript alone was P98 and that the video hadn't been tendered. In fact, I think it's right to say that P98 is the video and the transcript. Either way, we objected to it when it was tendered. So it makes ill difference, but that's one correction which should be entered. As far as the motion is concerned, I trust that it's largely self-explanatory. And it may be that the Prosecution may want to give a considered written response. I'm not sure entirely how we'll proceed from here. But for our part, when we were notified that the Prosecution intended to use this exhibit, given that we had objected to its admission into evidence on the 8th of October, 2004, we considered it appropriate to file a motion immediately to set out on the record what our objections are. The factual reasons are set out in part 3 of the motion of which you have courtesy copies, and I won't rehearse that here because it's set out, numbers 1 to 7, small Roman numerals 1 to 7. We don't know which part of the video, of course, the Prosecution intends to show to this witness and for what purpose. Indeed, it was even indicated to us that the Prosecution might not necessarily use this exhibit at all. It's a potential exhibit. So of course if the Prosecution have since decided not to use this exhibit with this next witness, then the matter again would not need to be dealt with immediately. We were taken somewhat by surprise that this exhibit would be used with the next witness, Slavoljub Zikic - who is not a protected witness; I can mention his name - because he's not actually shown in the video at all, unlike the witness who comes after him, Mr. Radic, who is purported, at least, in the video. Now, it may be that the Prosecution want to use the video for identification purposes. Again, I don't know and I don't wish to speculate. But in that case, there would be no cause certainly for the transcript to be used or to be admitted -- not to be used for that witness or for the tape to be played. It's just simply a question of stopping it at a certain point for identification purposes. But nonetheless, we say that because of the features set out in 1 to 7, the tape should be excluded for all purposes, and that is, firstly, the prejudicial effect, we say, outweighs the probative value of the videotape and therefore should be excluded under 89(D). It's a strange interview with prompts and edits and other features which cast doubt on the -- both the authenticity and the reliability of the video. Secondly, under Rule 95, it may be that these interviews were obtained by oppression. And in that context, we would ask what are these people doing interviewing people who were visibly tired, in some cases injured, interviewing them without, it appears, the proper safeguards which would be normally adopted in such a situation? In the law of the former Yugoslavia, there were circumstances under which a person who may be tired and need medical treatment could be interviewed, but there are, of course, all sorts of safeguards to ensure that that's being properly done and that the whole interview isn't tainted by the condition that the person is in when being interviewed. So we say there are indices of oppression, and therefore we're in Rule 95 territory, and that therefore the video should be excluded unless the Prosecution satisfy you beyond a reasonable doubt, in accordance with your order, that the interviews were not obtained by oppression. And again, that might be going further ahead than we need to now because it depends a lot on what purpose the Prosecution want to use the video for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is going to respond to that? Ms. Richardson, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Your Honour, I will provide an oral response to this motion that was just filed by Defence counsel. I would like to add for the record that the Prosecution will reserve its rights to respond in writing, as we were just given this a few minutes ago. And I would certainly like to suggest, or request, that in the future, counsel would give us this -- any motions that they have in the morning hours, and we may very well be able to provide a response to it. But under the circumstances in the 25 minutes I will provide an oral response, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's be practical about it, Ms. Richardson. Could you for the time being restrict your oral response to what is relevant for the purpose of this particular witness, and then you will have every opportunity to respond in writing with regard to the rest of the submissions that are being put forward by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The first point I would like to make with respect to whether or not this -- the purpose for which this video will be used. The next witness, Mr. Zikic, will be testifying about his experiences in the police station and with respect to the other individuals he was kept captive. He -- the video will be used for purposes of identification, as well as verification of the injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Verification of whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Of the other prisoners, Your Honour. In fact, he is not on the video himself, but the purpose of showing him the video will be for him to identify his fellow prisoners, as well as the injuries that they received at the time of the exchange, which there is a date on the video itself. The next witness that the Prosecution will present is Mr. Radic, who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget Mr. Radic. That you may include when you file your written response.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just restrict yourself to Zikic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour. Thank you. Certainly with respect to the probative value of this videotape, I don't think -- it would be very difficult for one to imagine any other evidence of more probative value as the next individual will be testifying to the injuries that he observed, that he himself had, as well as what he observed his fellow prisoners to have. And it goes directly -- it certainly is relevant and probative. It goes directly to the beatings as alleged and the cruelty as alleged in the Prosecution's indictment. The reliability of it, Your Honour, can be tested through examination, as well as by cross-examination as well, the authenticity of it, Your Honour, can also be verified by the witnesses themselves, who -- the one tomorrow, Your Honour, was present when in fact it was taken. So I would have to say that any arguments with respect to oppressiveness and the conditions under which they were taken is pure speculation at this point by the Defence. In fact, one would argue that the time to take the video was immediately after these individuals were released from prison to document their injuries, and to get their evidence as to what happened to them. So I think the timeliness of it adds to its probative, relevant and reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my last point with respect to the translation, the Prosecution concedes that in fact the translation of the tape, we do need to have another translation conducted because it is -- there are some mistakes that we have found, but nonetheless, with respect to the witness and their testimony, the visibility of what is being shown to them, they can certainly verify and attest to and corroborate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not satisfied, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for a ruling from the Chamber. Just two points in reply. We don't accept it's the date which is shown on the video, at least that that's conclusive of when it was filmed. This next witness wasn't present when the interviews were conducted, so he can't help us with that. Conversely, he can describe the injuries which he saw on other prisoners and then that can be compared by Your Honours with what one sees on the video. But finally, if Your Honours are minded to rule against me and to allow the video to be shown for identification purposes alone, then I would simply repeat my submission that that doesn't require the transcript and the video can simply be frozen. It doesn't need to be played at any length. I'm obliged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our position is as follows: What we are going to decide today only refers to the use of this videotape with the witness Mr. Zikic, Slavoljub Zikic. The Chamber, of course, reserves its position with regard to the use of this tape with other witnesses until after it has been served with a copy of your written response. With regard to the use of this tape for the purpose of the testimony of Mr. Zikic, we have heard what -- we have taken into consideration the points raised by the Defence in their motion, of which the Trial Chamber had a courtesy copy and for which we thank the Defence. We have also taken note your response so far as it is limited to this particular witness. We are going to admit the use of this video recording for the purpose of the testimony which is about to start, with, of course, the caveat that the points raised by the Defence, as they may or may not relate to the probative value and authenticity of this document will be taken into consideration in due course when we come to evaluate the totality of the evidence that would have been furnished to this Trial Chamber in the course of this trial. So our decision is that you may make use of this video and we will have also a final say on the merit once we have taken cognizance of all the other points that you would like to raise in your written response. So any further matters before we admit the witness? Usher, could you please bring in the witness. To your knowledge, Ms. Richardson, does this witness have any problems with eyesight, hearing?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to this witness, Mr. Zikic does have a hearing problem. We may need to increase the volume on his headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: With respect to his eyesight, he does wear glasses, and I'm told that they are not -- it hasn't been updated recently. So they are of poor quality. But I don't think it will be a problem if the Court gives him considerable time to study any documents beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he is literate?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And he is literate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Zikic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, gentlemen, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed any further, since I am speaking in English, I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying in your own language, in a language, in other words, that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So far, so good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zikic. You are about to start giving evidence as a witness brought forward by the Prosecution in this case that has been instituted against Naser Oric. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. To help you make this declaration, the young lady who is standing next to you is going to hand to you the text of the solemn declaration, and I kindly ask you to read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn declaration and your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zikic. You may sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, today you are going to be here only for a few minutes, roughly about 20 minutes, and then we will continue and hopefully finish tomorrow. The procedure to be followed is a very simple one. You are first going to be asked a series of questions by Ms. Richardson, who I suppose you have already met. Then Ms. Richardson will be followed by Mr. Jones, who is one of the lawyers appearing for Naser Oric. You have a responsibility, an obligation, to answer all the questions that are put to you, as fully and as truthfully as possible, regardless of who is putting the question. In other words, you do not make a distinction between questions that are put to you by the Prosecution and questions that are put to you by the Defence. Your duty, your responsibility, is to always give a truthful and full answer. Did I make myself clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, if at any time, because today I said you will be here for a few minutes. Tomorrow you will be here for hours. If at any time you need a break, you feel tired, please do draw our attention. We are the three Judges on this case. Judge Brydensholt from Denmark is to my right, Judge Albin Eser from Germany is at my left, and my name is Judge Agius and I come from Malta. We'll try to make your stay here in The Hague as comfortable as possible; at the same time, you try to answer all the questions that are put to you in the way that I have indicated to you so that you can get out of here as quickly as possible. Thank you. Ms. Richardson, you can lead the witness so far as the preliminary issues are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by MS. SELLERS:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Slavoljub Zikic, son of Milovan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are also known by the name Drago as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please confirm for the Trial Chamber the following information: You were born in 1935, you're married, and you have two children, and you are a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are the former manager of the Fakovici post office and -- until 1992, and you also had land upon which you planted crop, and you owned livestock?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was not the director, though. I was the manager or administrator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you presently retired from the post office?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you live in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, you lived in Fakovici with your wife, Milenka and your children?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your children reside in Fakovici or were they residing in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: In Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many houses are located in the village of Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that such questions would be asked. I could have prepared for that. But I think it was between 30 and 40 houses in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this a purely Serb village, at least in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: A purely Serb village before and after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what types of buildings were located in the village of Fakovici in 1992. Did you have a school, a police station, a farming cooperative, and other types of public buildings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: We had two elementary schools, one communal hall, a health centre, one post office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the surrounding villages, are they Serb? Surrounding villages of Fakovici, are they Serb villages or are they Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: This is a little hard to explain. I can go one by one, if you allow me, just to mention some villages which are in the territory of that local commune, my local commune of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: I will start along the Drina River, the settlements along the Drina. Tuk, Grabovica, Vranesevici, Popovici, Vesici, Fakovici, which is where I come from, followed by a Muslim settlement one kilometre from Fakovici, called Zanjevo. Then Serb villages continue on, Divovici, Radijevici, Boljevici, Kutijesi. Then in the Brdo area, there were some Muslim settlements, Koseva [phoen], Jagodnja, Poznanovici. The other villages then belong to the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now, with respect to the Muslim villages, how far away from Fakovici is the closest Muslim village, and could you give us the name of that village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: The closest Muslim village along the Drina to Fakovici is Zanjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zikic --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to change your answer or do you want to add something in addition to Zanjevo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: The only village next to the Drina is Zanjevo, called Abdulici. It actually has two names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if -- I would like to take you back to 1992 or prior to 1992. Did you have good relations with your Muslim neighbours, the Muslims that lived in the neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: I have land left to me by my father in the village of Zanjevo itself and I would go there to do some farming work. The neighbours from Zanjevo would say: This is not for you. You're a manager. You don't know how to do it. Then they would come to my aid, they would help me, and I would just sit there and smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you didn't have any problems with your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever. I never had any problems with them in my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, did there come a time that there was some tension with your Muslim neighbours, and do you remember when this began?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC
utterances.text: I really didn't pay attention to that, but I think in 1991, when everything started in Croatia, I think that both the Serbs and the Muslims secretly received the odd rifle in order to carry out village guard duty.
